title: The Goddess in all beings
hookLine: a red book read aloud before sunrise for nine mornings, and the hymn at its heart: the Goddess in all beings
carry: shakti: the goddess lives in all beings as power
tomorrow: Kanya puja: girls as the Goddess
last: HOLI: GOD PLAYS, AND LOVE PLAYS BACK.

cards: Before sunrise, in a small kitchen in Kolkata, a grandmother sits on a low stool with a red cloth-bound book open on her knees.
She reads aloud in Sanskrit, fast and steady, the way you read something you've read every autumn of your life. A lamp burns beside her. She'll do this every morning until the ninth.
Inside are the battles you heard on day eighty-seven. But today, one hymn from the middle of the book, sung by gods who had lost everything.

teach.b: The book is the Devi Mahatmya, the Glory of the Goddess. Many families read it, or have a priest read it, across the nine nights; it also goes by Durga Saptashati, the seven hundred, after its traditional count of verses.

It tells three battles, and in the third there's a scene. Two demon brothers, Shumbha and Nishumbha, have taken heaven. The gods, thrown out, climb into the Himalaya and do the only thing left: they praise the Goddess.

teach.h: THE GODS' HYMN: IN ALL BEINGS.
teach.b: Their hymn is one of the most loved in Hinduism. Line after line, they bow to the Goddess who lives in all beings: as consciousness, as sleep, as hunger, as strength, as patience, as faith, as compassion, as mother.

teach.h: WE BOW TO HER, AGAIN AND AGAIN.
teach.b: And every line ends the same way: we bow to her, we bow to her, again and again. Just then Parvati comes down to bathe in the river. Whom are you praising? she asks.
And out of her own body steps another goddess, shining, who answers: they're praising me. Then she goes out to meet the brothers. Here's the teaching under the festival.
The Goddess is Shakti, power itself: not only a figure riding a lion, but the strength inside every living thing, even sleep, hunger, a mother's care.
That's why the nights are kept for nine forms, the Navadurga, one each night, from Shailaputri, daughter of the mountain, to Siddhidatri, who gives perfection.
Many families greet her with Jai Mata Di, victory to the Mother.
The same power, nine faces, and the same power in the people in your own house.

how: During Navaratri many Hindus read or recite the Devi Mahatmya (the Durga Saptashati) across the nine nights and honor the Goddess in nine forms, the Navadurga, one each night, with fasting and prayers; the tenth day, Vijayadashami or Dussehra, celebrates victory.

o: nine nights honoring the Goddess in nine forms
nine nights of fireworks for a king's crowning
a nine-day market for selling the new harvest

it tells three battles: Madhu and Kaitabha, Mahishasura, and Shumbha and Nishumbha.
many families read the Devi Mahatmya across the nine nights
sometimes all of it, sometimes a part each day, at home or with a priest.

games.q: you're one of the gods. Shumbha and Nishumbha have thrown you out of heaven. what do you do?
o: build your own army and try again.
praise the Goddess who lives in all beings.
make a deal with the brothers.
games.why: the gods sing to the Goddess who lives in all beings as power. she steps out of Parvati's body and answers: they're praising me.

practice: Sit with the lamp, the way the grandmother does. If you pray, say Jai Mata Di softly, or the hymn's refrain: we bow to her, again and again.
Then think of the strength in one ordinary person near you: a grandmother's patience, a friend's nerve, your own tired body still going. In Navaratri's eyes, that's her. Bow to it inside.
If you don't pray, simply notice it, and be grateful for it.

wordCard.voice: Navaratri. Nine nights of the Goddess, kept with her book read aloud and one of her nine forms honored each night.

orig.note: Sanskrit devīmāhātmya: devī, the Goddess, and māhātmya, greatness, glory.

carryVoice: Your line: shakti. The Goddess lives in all beings as power. That's day one hundred forty-three.

sources.ref: Devi Mahatmya (Markandeya Purana): ch. 5 (the gods' hymn to the Goddess who abides in all beings; the Goddess emerges from Parvati's body), chs. 1–10 (the three battles)
